On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, as there probably will not be time to have a question answered1 in the regular way, I would ask the Postmaster General to state how many tenders have been received for the Yukon mail contract, the names of those who have tendered, the amount of each tender, and the successful tenderer.

Mr. Speaker, the bon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) consulted with me before deciding to ask this question, and I have an answer prepared. Nine tenders have been received, as follows:
Gorst Air Transport Limited-$750 per round trip carrying 1,000 pounds of mail each way with at least 50 round trips per season, $37,-500.-And any trips in excess of 50 will he carried for $650 per trip (round), 1,000 pounds.
The department asked that tenders be submitted for the carrying of 62,000 pounds of mail. This tender would amount to $45,300 for 62,000 pounds. The following tenders were for the full tonnage of mail:
Thomas Cecil Richards Whitehorse, $44,000. P. Martin and J. R. Alguire, $45,000.
John L. McLennan, A. Dubois and E. E. Hickey, $49,750.	.
J. E. Greenfield and J. E. Pickering (Greenfield and Pickering) Whitehorse, $56,000. Christian Gloslie, $56,900.
George Camden Smith, Whitehorse, Yukon; $57 250.
Greenfield and Pickering, Whitehorse, (J. E. Greenfield and J. E. PickeTing), $60,000. Robert Lowe, Whitehorse, $60,000.
Those are the nine tenders. The question was to whom the contract would be awarded.
The contract was awarded to the lowest tenderer, namely, Thomas Cecil Richards, Whitehorse, $44,000.
For the information of the house I may say that since they brought uip the question of carrying increased poundage, I have looked into the matter and it appears that a certain quantity of second-class matter accumulates during the winter time at Dawson or Whitehorse and is not transferred to the Yukon until some time in the spring or summer. I am endeavouring to make arrangements with the man who has been awarded this contract under the general call, to have that extra accumulated mail taken over at certain periods as it accumulates, perhaps once a month, and, if possible, twice a month. If that cannot be done in the regular way by the trail, we will endeavour to have it done by aeroplane so that when the spring arrives there will be very little, if any, accumulated mail for that section of the country.
The question has been raised of having that mail service carried out by aeroplane. I have not accepted that suggestion for the reason that if we accept the proposition of transporting mail to the Yukon entirely by aeroplane, we shall be taking away from the people of the Yukon the assistance they are now getting through a mail contract, of keeping the trail open in the winter .time. By this system of transportation of the mail we aid that territory by keeping open the winter trail, and I thought it in the interests of the people there, while permitting a certain amount to be carried by aeroplane, to continue the old system of getting the mail through in order to assist those people by keeping the trail open during the winter.

Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 313, to amend the Dominion Elections Act. He said: The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), the chairman of the committee, will, I think, be in a better position than I am to explain the amendments to the house.

There are a few amendments which are really corrections of typographical errors which have crept into the printed copy. One amendment of a very serious nature is the following. The clause reads:
Dominion Elections Act

Any appointment made by the chief electoral officer may be made by reference to the title of office of the appointee.
The Senate in their revising capacity have thought well to make it read:
By reference to the title of the office.
There is some discussion amongst authorities learned in the law as to whether or not we should say a man has the title of office or the title of the office. In view, however, of the importance of the legislation, I would not suggest to the house that we appoint managers to consult with the Senate as to whether this matter was seriously discussed with them. The other amendments are not of any consequence and I suggest that the house accept them.
Motion agreed to, amendments read the second time and concurred in.

Yesterday we had a good deal of discussion with regard to clearance papers for vessels carrying liquor to the United States. If the government carried out the expressed wishes of this parliament in 1926 and refused clearance papers to such vessels, what difference would it make to the revenue of this country? If clearance papers were refused, would it cost a great deal, and if so, how much, in the minister's estimation, for any increased force that would have to be engaged to do this work?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
I am not sure -that I can give anything like an accurate estimate of the amount of revenue that would be lost if clearances were discontinued. It might not be very great. The committee, of course, understands that all excise is paid on liquor when it leaves the distilleries. The collections last year of liquor cleared for the United States amounted to $12,421,000. If those clearances were discontinued, I do not think it would at all follow that a large amount of liquor would not go to the United States, and whether it entered the United States by way of clearance or without a clearance, that liquor, if it came from Canadian distilleries, would still have paid us revenue, but it would not then appear under the heading of clearances to the United States, because clearances would

not be granted. It would appear, no doubt, as domestic consumption. The liquor would be purchased, I suppose, from the government stores in Ontario or from the liquor commission in Quebec. It might be exported and yet it would not appear under clearances to the United States, so that we could not calculate what amount would be lost. It would all depend upon how much the exportation to the United States would foe reduced by the discontinuance of clearances.
The other question, I understand, was how much it would cost
For an extra force to try to prevent people from breaking the law with regard to importing liquor into the United States.

I cannot say definitely. I have heard it estimated at anywhere from $1,000,000 upward a year. It would depend upon the size of the preventive force you would require to establish. You might have to put boats on the lakes in order to watch vessels going out illegally without clearances.
Will the minister give the house the increase in the preventive service in the last three years?

In the land forces in 1927,
there were 142 employees, and in 1928, 342. It was in 1928 that the chief reorganization took place. Last year there were 318 employees, a slight reduction, as compared) with the previous year. The personnel of the shipping crews amounted in 1927 to 283; 1928, 649; 1929, 644. To the latter should be added 48 men for two new vessels now building, one of which I understand will soon be in commission. The number of employees on cruisers and patrol boats in 1927 was 16, and in 1928, 39.

What was

I have just given those
figures.

There is no doubt that the minister is doing something to try to straighten out the preventive service. I notice that in 1922-23 the total number of employees, according to the figures furnished me by the department, was 127. What the figure of the minister is for that year I do not know. In 1923-24 the total was 170; 1924-25, 186; 1925-26, 299; 1926-27, 400; for
the first nine months of 1927-28, 662. So there has been a very heavy increase in recent years. One would expect that there would be quite a 'bit more in seizure collections. It may be, however, that the mere establishment of the preventive service has had the effect of curtailing smuggling to some degree.

That is the meaning of the
word preventive.

Exactly,
but I am at a loss to understand' one very striking comparison that I have before me. In the year 1923-24, the total customs seizures amounted to 8334,877, and excise seizures, 8268,148, or a total of $603,026. Those are the figures given me by the department. That total amount of seizures, $603,026, was made with a total staff of 170. In 1926-27, almost exactly the same amount of seizures was made, namely, S429,603, but that required 400 men, or at least 400 men were employed. In 1923, 170 men made seizures amounting to 8603,026, and in 1926-27, 400 men seized approximately the same amount.

The answer simply is this:
The preventive service was doing what they were supposed to do, preventing smuggling. If smuggling were not going on, there would be fewer seizures.

If that is
the case, take the year immediately preceding in each case. In 1922-23, with a staff of 127 men, the seizures amounted to $326,434. Either the staff was not doing its duty at that time or there was very little smuggling. The attempted smuggling must have very much increased next year or the staff improved its service, one or the other, to collect the enormous amount they did that year. Between 1923-24 and 1924-25 there is a drop of $200,000 in the seizures. There seems to be a very striking fluctuation in the activities of the preventive service.

Not within the last few
years.
The figures are striking because in the year 1922-23 the seizures amounted to $300,000 and in 1923-24 to $600,000, and in 1926-27 to $429,000.
If a big seizure of liquor is made it runs into money. Sometimes you may get seizures periodically and sometimes none at all.

The minister will perhaps not overlook the fact that seizures of liquor are tabulated separately, I
Supply-National Revenue

understand, because I find at the foot of one of these columns a note that, in addition, 70,534 gallons of liquor were seized having a duty paid value of $830,000. It does not say for what year that was.

I might be permitted to
say a word or two on the preventive service, on the increase in the personnel, and on the variations in the value of the seizures in 192324, and in 1927, when the staff was larger. I think it is well known to the house that I live in a seaport myself. The county which I have the honour to represent is situated partly in the Restigouche Bay, partly in the baie des Ohaleurs, and partly in the gulf of the St. Lawrence. Included in the lower section of the county we have Shippigan island and Miscou island, part of one island being entirely in the baie des Chaleurs and the other island drawing an imaginary line from East Point, Miscou, to Point Maquereau on the Quebec side, half in the gulf of St. Lawrence and half in the baie des Chaleurs. The balance of the county from these islands down to the county line of Northumberland is entirely in the gulf of St. Lawrence. I myself served in the customs department for eleven years as chief collector of the port of Bathurst, having under me four or five outports. During those years we had trouble with smuggling, and we had no organization to cope with it except the ordinary customs officials and tide waiters. There was no such thing between 1900 and 1911 as a real preventive service to stop smuggling on the high seas. Whatever the department did at that time was done through the officials who had their land duties to perform, which took up most of their time. When prohibition came into force in the several provinces down by the Atlantic seaboard smuggling increased, especially after the high duties placed on imported liquors. Up to 1925 there was not a sufficient staff to prevent smuggling to any great extent. The fishing fleets of the islands of Miscou and Shippigan in the county of Gloucester, numbering some 350 sail, would leave their home ports on a Monday and go codfishing on the banks in the strait of Northumberland, remaining away the whole week. At that time there was what was known as a " rum row " not only in the gulf of St. Lawrence and the Northumberland strait but also in the baie des Chaleurs. Our fishermen could get all the liquor they wanted at a very low price in exchange for their fish. When those men arrived home on Saturday they had smuggled liquor galore for distribution and sale. After the organization of the preventive force which 
the minister now has at his disposal, on that section of the New Brunswick coast rum row disappeared; we are no longer bothered with vessels lying twelve or fourteen miles out in the gulf of St. Lawrence or in the baie des Chaleurs loaded down with liquor ready to be handed over the side to fast motor boats. Since 1926 smuggling has disappeared in that lower section of the baie des Chaleurs and the gulf of St. Lawrence. I am not going to speak of conditions in the strait of Northumberland, that locality being too far away from my home. In those two areas smuggling has been reduced at least 80 per cent, and to-day we in the county of Gloucester are proud to be able to say that there is no smuggled liquor to be found in the homes of our fishermen.
I wish now to compliment the minister and his officials on the way in which they have organized the preventive service in that, section of New Brunswick. In the past smuggling had the effect of demoralizing our fishermen; to-day we are clear of it. Under the old system we had no preventive officers in any of the outports in the county of Gloucester. There were five outports and one main port, and the only preventive officer we had was the preventive man or tide waiter in the port of Bathurst. To-day, if I am not mistaken, we have not only some four or five land preventive officers, but we have well manned and fast patrol boats. The result is that the smuggling fraternity, knowing those waters are so well .patrolled, no longer look to that section of New Brunswick as a haven for their operations. At the present time there are ninety per cent fewer seizures, not because the officials are failing to do their work, but because they are doing it so effectually that the baie des Chaleurs and the gulf of St. Lawrence is clear of smuggling, to the credit of the Department of National Revenue and to the glory of the counties bordering on those waters. That will explain to some extent why with a staff of three or four hundred as compared with the former staff of about two hundred, fewer seizures are being made. The fewer seizures made the better it is for the country, provided the organization is operating as efficiently in other sections of .the Dominion as it is in the section to which I have referred in the maritime provinces. I take it that it is not so much a question of the department getting revenue out of seizures as of preventing liquor from being trafficked in on the high seas.
The minister's statement is very interesting, but the point I wanted to make was not that there is

There is a considerable
reduction in the number of seizures if you compare the traffic of 1925 to 1926, as we knew it living along the seaboard, to what it was in 1922 and 1923.

been cut down.

If he will let me know a

-the best he can buy, if he can discover any smuggling of that kind along the shores that I have just named.

ing salaries, $1,038,319.34; patrol cars purchased. $40,881.22; land officers' salaries, $528,366.37; travelling expenses, $42,566.45. This makes the total.
Does the minister believe that he has now reached the limit of his requirements in the preventive service? Is the thing pretty well checked now?

It should be less, so far as expenditure is concerned, because in these figures there are sums paid for boats. We are building two final boats now and hope these will meet the requirements, so that next year the estimates may perhaps be less. I do not care to make that statement too definitely because we cannot tell what developments may occur which we shall have to meet; but I should judge that in future we should have a smaller estimate than this year's.

The minister might circumscribe his remarks by his mention of the number of boats. What about the personnel, the staff itself? The increase has been considerable; in the last feiw years the number has increased from 186 to over 600. I wonder whether the minister has any idea as to when the limit will be reached. I have no doubt he is doing good work and knows just, how well the preventive service is functioning. The excise seizures are falling off, I assume he believes that, although I do not know whether it is a fact. As a matter of fact, are the excise and customs seizures falling off?
The excise seizures in 1927 were 1,618 and in 1928, 1,148.
What about the value?
I have not that. It would hardly 'be a question of value, because where an illicit still is seized there is no question of value.

Well, how does the department get the figures if the minister cannot supply them to me? The department says that in 1926-27 the excise seizures were valued at $123,260, and in 192728, for nine months, $106,658. Perhaps the minister will check up those figures.
The commissioner informs me that there is an appraised value taken which is usually too high. I cannot add anything to that.
The minister cannot answer.
What is the exact question?
The exact question is as to the total value of the excise seizures made in 1928-29.
We have not got it here but can get it.
The minister has the figures for the salaries, for the boats, for the employees and the expenses; the only thing he lacks is the value of the excise seizures.
It would be only an estimated value in any case.

That was not suggested in the reply given to me by the department. The figures from the department are very definite; they are given in two columns, side by side, the total value of customs seizures and the total value of excise seizures. There is no question of an approximation; the exact figures are given. I must presume that documents from the department are accurate and not deceiving.

The significant fact is the
number of seizures made. But when a still is seized it is destroyed and whatever alcohol is there is also destroyed, so that the value disappears.

On what
basis does the minister estimate his requirements in the way of personnel, staff, boats and so forth for the period immediately succeeding? He does not jump at a conclusion and say, "We shall require 1,000 men and 200 boats". He estimates the amount of work to be done and1, I presume, he also estimates the number of men required to conduct the preventive service properly and efficiently; then he puts in his estimate. What I want to know is this: Does the minister think that we have now reached the limit?
I have answered that question.

Yes; but
on what does the minister base his opinion?
On experience, of course.

But that
varies.

The experience of a practical man, I should say, would be a pretty good indication. If we know that last year the number of men we had was about right, we shall know that that is what we ought to

have in the following year; and if, during the following year, developments show that we have either too many or too few, we shall make our adjustments accordingly. That is ordinary common sense.

But the
expenditure, you see, is going up.
It includes capital expenditure for the construction of boats, which capital expenditure I said would no longer be required to be included inasmuch as the department would have all the boats needed.

What is
the capital expenditure on the boats alone?

We are building two new
cruisers this year, costing $600,000-$300,000 each. That is entirely capital and that will not be needed next year.
What is the tonnage of the new cruisers, and what speed will they have?

They will have a speed of
17 knots; as to the tonnage, I am not much of a nautical man and I do not know. The speed' is 17 knots and the crews will number 24 each. The length is 165 feet, the breadth 21 and the depth 13 feet.

How does that speed
compare with that of the boats chased?

In the outside service it
compares favourably with the speed of the large boats that come into the 12 mile limit, where these large boats operate. The small launches and speed boats that engage in smuggling within that limit are of course faster, but we have some boats to compete with them, attaining as high a speed as 35 miles an hour.

Will the
minister give the total number of excise and customs seizures by provinces?

The excise seizures by provinces last year were: Prince Edward Island, 40; Nova Scotia, 64; New Brunswick, 21; Quebec, 328; Ontario, 312; Manitoba, 120; Saskatchewan, 202; Alberta, 41; British Columbia, 20; Yukon, none-making a total of 1,148.

How do you account for
the small number of seizures in British Columbia, only half as many as those made in Alberta?

British Columbia is a
difficult territory to operate in.

seizures by provinces?

The commissioner is trying
to get that information; I will have it in a moment.

I have listened with great interest to this debate and to the statement made by the minister. With reference to the recommendations made by the special committee of this parliament in 1926 and the recommendations of the royal commission, I notice that a great many of the recommendations have been carried out, but one which was made both by the commission and the special committee in connection with the refusal of clearance papers for boats carrying liquor to the United States apparently has been entirely ignored, and as yet I have not heard a clear and definite statement from the minister as to why this recommendation has not been complied with. It seems to me this is the most important point in the discussion, and I should be glad if the minister could give us a clear statement as to why that recommendation has not been followed.

I have given the explanation, but I will give it again. I think I made very clear what perhaps was not well understood by the committee or by members of the house, that clearances cannot be refused under the present law; that is the opinion of the Department of Justice. In order to refuse clearances, therefore, it would be necessary to amend the law by an act of parliament, and I am not sure that this was the intention at that time. I will say, however, that we have made many changes according to the recommendations contained in these reports, as we thought advisable in the light of experience and what we thought was necessary. If this parliament decides that clearances should be refused, then parliament will have to enact new legislation, and I will say to my hon. friend that personally I do not feel that advisable at the moment, for reasons which I gave in a former address some two weeks ago. I would say further that even during this debate I have found no reason to believe that this parliament, which at the moment is in the control of the destinies of this country, desires that change to be made; I have had no intimation from parliament or at least from more than a limited number of members that they desire any such change in the law.

To me it seems an extraordinary statement that at present clear-
Supply-National Revenue-

ance papers cannot be refused under the law. Is it not a fact that some of the commissioners who conducted that inquiry were learned legal gentlemen, who were paid fabulous fees for their services? If that is so why should they make recommendations apparently in ignorance of the laws of the country?

I am sure my hon. friend
does not suggest that even judges are infallible.
I do suggest that if we are to pay such men $150 a day or more, certainly they should understand what they are recommending to this parliament.

So far as the department
is concerned there is no doubt whatever that under the present law we cannot refuse clearances. I think my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, who acted as minister of this department for a short time, desired to refuse these clearances, but he also found that under the present law he could not do so. I personally made inquiries in that regard and was informed by the Department of Justice, whose guidance we must accept in matters of law, that under the law as it stands now there is no authority for the minister to refuse these clearances.
The government has already undertaken to reduce the number of docks from which clearances may be made, and I was wondering why these docks could not be eliminated altogether.

As I explained some time
ago, when the excise is paid on the liquor it becomes free, as is the case with any other commodity; it is in the same category as any other article which may be legally exported from Canada, and where a customs port exists anyone may avail himself of that port for the purpose of making exports. While we can limit the number of docks within a port we can do nothing which will prohibit any legal commodity from passing through that port. For instance, within the confines of the Windsor district there were some forty or fifty docks from which liquor went out. We cannot stop the liquor going out from that port but we can tell the exporters that they can ship only from certain designated docks, although of course that has not the prohibitory effect. Shipments may be carried on, but the traffic may be limited in that way, which also gives us more control.

I am sorry I have not that information.

I have heard a good deal
of discussion, particularly from this section of the house, with regard to this question of refusing clearances. I am not going to discuss it at any length, but I want to say that I think if we began refusing clearances we would get into a great deal of real trouble. I should like to suggest to those people who are interested in preventing liquor from going to the United States that they go a little further and advocate prohibiting the manufacture of liquor in Canada, or as an alternative, suggest that the government control the whole business. Then we would not be faced with this question of refusing clearances, and we would not be permitting individual corporations to make money out of the business. Otherwise Canada will have to assume a large responsibility and a considerable expenditure to try to enforce a law which we have proved to be at least very difficult if not almost impossible to enforce.
If the house should decide to abolish the manufacture of liquor in Caanda where would the political parties obtain their campaign funds?

That is a question I will
have to relay across the floor to the government and to the acting leader of the opposition; I do not know anything about such matters. If it so happens that the party campaign funds come from that source, they might be considerably reduced if we abolished the manufacture of liquor, but that might be a good thing and I do not think that is a reason why we should not take that step. However, I have every confidence in the present Minister of National Revenue; I think he is doing his work very well and I think the people of Canada believe that the Department of National Revenue is perhaps


Supply-National Revenue
the most efficient department of government to-day. Just in closing I might add that personally I am opposed to the drink traffic. I do not think that we can assist the United States government very much by refusing these clearances; we would be making a great deal of trouble for ourselves. I am going to suggest, as the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) suggested last night, that the government consider a more fundamental way of dealing with this matter. I believe the people of Canada should take over the whole business and nationalize the traffic with a view to abolishing it as soon as possible. Those who have become so accustomed to drinking that they cannot live without it will soon die off and younger people will be coming along who do not require liquor, and we can get rid of the whole business. I think the only course which can be followed is the one the minister is following, and I suggest to him that this question of nationalization be considered. I do not think that prohibition will be successful because it seems to be very difficult to enforce and I think the same results would be obtained through nationalization of the business. In that way the supply could be stopped at its source and we would have full control over the traffic.

Mr. Chairman, a few
days ago the minister took a very strong stand in regard to the enforcement of the law as it concerns the government of the United Slates, and I hope he will not do anything to weaken that position. The majority of the people of Canada, irrespective of province, party or race, as well as many people in the United States, support his position. Some people take the opposite view, quite sincerely no doubt, and I respect them, but there has been too much hypocrisy introduced into this question. Of course if one believes that Canadians have come down to the low level of the decadent and degraded races of the world, and find it impossible to control their habits of drinking, then one is right in asking for prohibition, but I am one of those who believe that we still retain some of the elements of civilization and are able to control our own habits in matters of drinking, as well as eating or anything else. Blue laws such as were necessary to be enacted by the French government in dealing with the Indians in the early days are not required to moralize the people of Canada. If people believe that the white population of this country has reached a point where the Indian population was centuries ago, or the Negro tribes of Africa are at the present time, then they are right in asking for prohibition, but
the majority of the people of Canada still come up to the civilized standard of humanity and I do not think it is the business of the government to interfere with the ordinary habits of human beings.
I have no desire to throw any cold water upon the enthusiasm evinced by some members as to the effectiveness of our preventive service, and so forth, and I do believe that prevention is now much more effective than it was. However, there is another factor which must be considered, the fact that several of the provinces of Canada have come back to their senses and are now allowing a reasonable amount of controlled liquor traffic within their borders. This applies now to every province in Canada, Ontario as well as the western and the maritime provinces; they have come back to a normal standard in this matter. The Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) has made a good case for the province of New Brunswick, but I do not think the number of seizures in that province would have diminished as they have if it had stuck to its old policy of prohibition.
As was pointed out to the minister last year, another factor in the increase of smuggling and the manufacture of moonshine liquor is the high duties which were imposed upon liquor during the war times. Last year the minister intimated that the time might come when these duties would be decreased. A few weeks ago I received a letter from a missionary who has been stationed in northern Ontario for many years. He deals especially with the Indian tribes and asked me if it would not be possible for the government to do something to prevent the enormous amount of bad alcohol which is being distributed among the Indians of Manitoulin island and along the northern shore of lake Superior. He told me that he had been in that district for years and had noticed a very marked increase in the supply of bad whiskey ever since the high duties had been imposed. He said that before that time there was some drunkenness among the Indians but there was not the same inducement to illicit traffic as was given by the imposition of these high taxes. The minister intimated last year that he might take the sense of the house with regard to the lowering of these duties, and I think he would do well in not losing sight of that suggestion.
The position taken 'by the minister and his department with regard to the issuance of clearance papers is, in my estimation, the right one to take. I marvel at the way some people in Canada boast of our .national pride but then seem to be prepared to make the officials of the Canadian government police agents for

the United States. I have no desire whatever to put Canada in a state of aloofness or difficulty with the government of the United States, but even the people in the United States realize that Canada is not on the northern border of their .country simply as a police station for the American government. Mr. La Guardia, when speaking in the House of Representatives last week, said that the government of the United States was handicapped in putting its own laws into operation in the state of Maine because some of the best people in that state were the real lawbreakers. W'hat justice would there be, and what sense would there be in asking the Canadian government to use its public services to enable the government of the United States to enforce a law which they are unable, and a good many of their agents are unwilling, to enforce in the United States. It has been demonstrated by public inquiries that the agents of the government of the United States are themselves smugglers into their own country.
To come back to our own country: my hon. friend from Bow River spoke of his experience in New Brunswick. I might speak of a similar experience I had in Ontario in holy prohibition days. I was once travelling through the western part of Ontario with a party of friends from Montreal. Some of us wanted to go ahead to prepare the reception in one of the inland towns. They were going at a pretty high speed in order to make time, when they saw a car coming after them and making certain signals which were understood by the chauffeur who said: "These are speed agents; I am afraid we will be held up for a fine.'' To this my friend said: "Very well, we will pay the fine and make the best we can out of it." So the police agents caime up and said: "Gentlemen, you are from the province of Quebec?" "Yes." "Well, we want to show our spirit of hospitality," so they took out of their car a case of beer and they said: "You know this is not-" what was that famous beer? -"two point four per cent?" I tasted it once and I will never taste it again. It is far worse than any kind of rum the hon. member for Bow River may have tasted in New Brunswick. They said: "This is real beer, made in Quebec." My friends were very thankful, and I cannot, any more than they did, blame the police agents for their generous spirit of hospitality. But this shows the difficulty of enforcing blue laws in any country whatever. I think one of the most sensible things that has been done by the Ferguson government is the amendment of their liquor laws, and if the number of seizures decrease in Ontario, this will be largely due to the

sensible policy of that government. I hope we will keep on that footing of common sense. We should not always endeavour to imitate what is done by the people of the United States or by any other people. Let us have laws that suit the conditions of the average Canadian and let us try to enforce such laws as are capable of enforcement. Let us not endeavour to make laws under the pretence of making people perfect. We are not perfect and we have no mandate to moralize by laws the people of Canada or the people of the United States.

For the simple reason that
